```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
has.seurat <- requireNamespace("SeuratObject", quietly = TRUE)
has.rhdf5  <- requireNamespace("rhdf5", quietly = TRUE)
has.arrow  <- requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE)
```

NICHESv2 scores ligand-receptor (LR) signaling between individual pairs of
cells. For each directed cell pair and each LR pair, it asks whether the sending
cell expresses the ligand and the receiving cell expresses the receptor. It
keeps every non-zero score, so you can trace a signal back to the exact cells
that produced it.

This vignette runs the whole workflow on a small synthetic dataset that ships
with the package, so every step takes a moment and needs no download.

```{r load}
library(NICHESv2)
library(data.table)
```

## Inputs

`create_NICHESObject()` needs three things: a gene-by-cell expression matrix,
cell metadata, and an LR database. The bundled `NICHESv2_inputs` list holds all
three, for 50 genes and 80 cells.

```{r inputs}
data(NICHESv2_inputs)
names(NICHESv2_inputs)

dim(NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx)
head(NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data, 3)
head(NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db, 3)
```

The column names of the matrix must match the row names of the metadata. Spatial
mode needs `x` and `y` columns in the metadata.

## Build a NICHESObject

Here each cell is connected to its spatial neighbors using `k = 5`. Only mutual
nearest neighbors become edges, and every cell also gets a self-loop for
autocrine signaling.

```{r create}
obj <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db    = NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db,
  mode      = "spatial",
  k         = 5L,
  method    = "product",
  verbose   = FALSE
)
dim(obj)
```

An edge is one directed cell pair. `method = "product"` multiplies the sender's
ligand expression by the receiver's receptor expression, and `"minimum"` takes
the smaller of the two. To use a fixed radius instead of `k`, pass `rad`;
`Explore_Radius_Neighborhood()` helps you choose a value.

For larger datasets, set `n.cores` to score LR pairs in parallel. This uses
socket clusters, so it works on every platform.

## Inside the object

A NICHESObject is a list with 15 slots, which you read with `$`.

| Level | Slots |
|---|---|
| Cell | `$cell.list`, `$cell.data`, `$cell.meta` |
| Edge | `$edge.list`, `$edge.data`, `$edge.meta` |
| Neighborhood | `$neighborhood.cell.list`, `$neighborhood.edge.list`, `$neighborhood.meta` |
| Gene and LRM | `$gene.list`, `$gene.meta`, `$LRM.list`, `$LRM.meta` |
| Extras | `$segmentation`, `$aggregations` |

Scores are stored in long format, with one row for each non-zero (edge, LRM)
pair. This keeps memory use tied to how much signal exists, not to the number of
possible combinations.

```{r edge-data}
head(obj$edge.data, 3)
```

Edge IDs have the form `"SendingCell|ReceivingCell"` and LRM IDs have the form
`"ligand|receptor"`. `$edge.data` is a `data.table`, so you can summarize it
directly. These are the strongest LR pairs overall:

```{r top-lrms}
obj$edge.data[, .(total.score = sum(score)), by = LRM][order(-total.score)][1:3]
```

`$edge.meta` carries each cell's metadata onto its edges, with `Sending.` and
`Receiving.` prefixes, which makes it easy to filter by cell type:

```{r edge-meta}
obj$edge.meta[, .N, by = .(Sending.celltype, Receiving.celltype)][1:3]
```

## Aggregate by neighborhood

Each cell's neighborhood is filled in when the object is built.
`aggregate_NICHESObject()` summarizes each one per LRM, and with `cell.type.col`
it also reports which cell types surround each cell.

```{r aggregate}
obj <- aggregate_NICHESObject(obj, cell.type.col = "celltype", verbose = FALSE)
names(obj$aggregations)
```

`$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg` has one row per (cell, LRM). It sorts each
neighborhood edge into five categories relative to the focal cell: `in`, `out`,
`cross` (between two neighbors), `self.autocrine` and `other.autocrine`.

```{r edge-agg}
agg <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg
agg[, .(cell, LRM, score.in.sum, score.out.sum, score.cross.sum)][1:3]
```

`$aggregations$neighborhood.composition` has one row per cell:

```{r composition}
comp <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.composition
comp[, .(cell, TypeA.neighbor.prop, TypeB.neighbor.prop, TypeC.neighbor.prop)][1:3]
```

## Subset to cells of interest

Aggregate first, then subset. Each retained cell keeps its neighborhood entries
and aggregation rows unchanged, so its values still describe its whole
neighborhood in the full tissue, including neighbors you didn't keep.

```{r subset}
type.a <- obj$cell.meta[celltype == "TypeA", cell]
sub <- obj[type.a]
dim(sub)

identical(
  sub$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg[, score.in.sum],
  agg[cell %in% type.a, score.in.sum]
)
```

The edge slots of a subset hold only edges between retained cells. Summing a
cell's rows in `sub$edge.data` can therefore give less than its aggregation row.

Because those removed edges are gone, aggregations can't be recomputed on the
subset, and trying stops with an error. To analyze the subset as a separate
tissue, rebuild its neighborhoods first:

```{r separate}
separate <- add_neighborhoods(sub, overwrite = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
separate <- aggregate_NICHESObject(separate, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Data without coordinates

For scRNA-seq data, `mode = "nonspatial"` pairs cells by random sampling within
each pair of cell types. It needs `cell.type.col`, and `seed` makes the sampling
repeatable.

```{r nonspatial}
ns <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx     = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db,
  mode          = "nonspatial",
  cell.type.col = "celltype",
  verbose       = FALSE
)
dim(ns)
```

For one summary per pair of cell types, use
`compute_PseudoBulk_Connectivity()`, which returns a `data.table`:

```{r pseudobulk}
pb <- compute_PseudoBulk_Connectivity(
  count.mtx     = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db,
  cell.type.col = "celltype",
  verbose       = FALSE
)
nrow(pb)
```

## Using your own data

### LR databases

Pass a database name to `LRM.db`, and set `species` to match your data.

```{r databases}
db <- load_LRM_database("connectomedb2025", species = "human", verbose = FALSE)
nrow(db)
```

`"connectomedb2025"` (the default in `load_LRM_database()`) and `"fantom5"` are
bundled for human, mouse, rat and pig. `"omnipath"` needs internet access and
the OmnipathR package, and covers human, mouse and rat. You can also pass your
own data frame. Multi-gene complexes are written with underscores, such as
`"COL1A1_COL1A2"`.

### Seurat objects

`extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat()` works with Seurat V4 and V5 objects. It returns
`count.mtx` and `meta.data`, ready for `create_NICHESObject()`. For spatial data,
add the coordinates to `meta.data` yourself as `x` and `y` columns.

```{r seurat, eval = has.seurat}
seu <- SeuratObject::CreateSeuratObject(
  counts    = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data
)
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat(seu, layer = "counts", verbose = FALSE)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)
```

The `layer` you choose sets what the scores mean: raw counts give absolute
magnitudes, and normalized expression gives relative scores.

### AnnData files

`extract_NICHESInputs_AnnData()` reads `.h5ad` files with rhdf5, so it doesn't
need Python.

```{r anndata, eval = has.rhdf5}
h5ad <- system.file("extdata", "NICHESv2_example.h5ad", package = "NICHESv2")
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_AnnData(h5ad, verbose = FALSE)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)
```

### Exporting to TissuePlex

`export_to_TissuePlex()` writes one Parquet file for interactive viewing of edges
in tissue coordinates. It needs the arrow package.

```{r tissueplex, eval = has.arrow}
out.file <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
export_to_TissuePlex(obj, output.path = out.file)
unlink(out.file)
```

`?add_neighborhood_edge_agg` for all 27 aggregation columns, and
`?"[.NICHESObject"` for the subsetting rules. `?NICHESv2` gives an overview.
